utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone inside the courtroom, also for those just outside the courtroom assisting us. Mr. Harmon, I see that you're the only one who represents the Prosecution today, and Mr. Stewart and Ms. Cmeric are there for the Defence. Are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Just before we begin, I would like to inform the Court for this abbreviated week we have three witnesses, two of whom will testify both on direct and cross-examination, and one of whom, 92 bis, will be available for cross-examination. I've talked to Mr. Stewart. We anticipate finishing the direct examination of Mr. Cengic, our first witness today. We believe that we will finish all three witnesses this week. Mr. Stewart has informed me he will commence his cross-examination possibly tomorrow on Mr. Cengic. Given that schedule, we are comfortable, both parties, that we will conclude all three witnesses today -- all three witnesses this week. Not today. This week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, if we would not start cross-examination today and if that would result in not finishing with all witnesses this week, then of course the Chamber might see this as a problem. But since both parties are still confident that according to their schedule, we'll finish all three witnesses this week, then we could start according to that schedule. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. The first witness will be Mr. Cengic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ismet Cengic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cengic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Cengic. Mr. Cengic, it will be Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution, who examines you first. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I would like to begin by going through your background, and the way I propose to proceed is I will state certain data and I will ask you to affirm the data as being correct. Let me begin, then, Mr. Cengic. You were born on the 1st of January, 1945, you are a citizen of Bosnia, and your faith is Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were educated in Bosnia, first at Gymnasium, later at the University of Sarajevo, where you studied at the faculty of natural sciences and earned a degree in mathematics; later, you were a professor of mathematics at the high school level in the years 1973 to 1976, 1978 to 1990, and 2001 to the present time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You served your compulsory military service in the JNA from September 1992 until September of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were a member of the SDA political party until the year 2001; you were a member of the Main Board of the SDA of the Novi Grad municipality until 2000; and you were a member of the SDA Main Board at the state level between September of 1997 and September of 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I proudly affirm so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were elected in 1990 as president of the Municipal Assembly of the municipality of Novi Grad; in January of 1996 you were elected by the Municipal Assembly to be the head of the municipality, that is the highest executive branch, head of that branch. Between 1997 and 2000, you were elected president of the municipal council of Novi Grad, and from 2000 to the present, you serve as a deputy on the Novi Grad council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a member of the council, in the council of the town of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, far be it for us to quarrel with something that both the witness and the Prosecution are happy with, but we do question the dates given in answer to what Mr. Harmon -- or Mr. Harmon's dates in relation to compulsory military service. We just wonder whether those are the correct dates. If they are, well, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps I misstated those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Cengic, when you served your compulsory military service in the JNA. I may have asked you the wrong dates.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: From September 1972 until September 1973.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I obviously stated the wrong dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Let us begin with the first exhibit, if we could, and I will need the assistance of the usher in displaying this particular exhibit. Just to inform Your Honours, this exhibit is a large map of the city of Sarajevo. It is unmarked. I present it because this witness will refer to certain locations on it. It may be of benefit to Your Honours in future testimony. I've left it blank so Your Honours can make whatever notations on it you want during this testimony of Mr. Cengic and other witnesses. And if I could have the assistance of the usher just to hold up the map so Mr. Cengic --.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, what I would like you to do: To your right on the table is a pointer. What I would like you to do, Mr. Cengic, if you would be so kind as to point on this map in just a moment, when the Judges have had an opportunity to open the maps. If the usher could turn just a bit so I could have a little bit of visual line of sight. Mr. Cengic, what I would like you to do on this map, just generally point to the area of the Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you do that again. I want the Judges to be able to see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's too of a big a map to put on the ELMO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just the general area.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: This is the boundary with Vogosca. Here at Paljevo, there is the boundary opposite which is Brijesce. And then we have the boundary with Ilidza, which runs along there. Ilidza is down there. This is the airfield belonging to Ilidza. On -- here lies Novo Sarajevo, in this area. This is the Ivan Krndelj street and if you run along that street, you follow the street and this is where it is. And it is -- and then on the right-hand side, it goes up until Otoka, along the Zrak company complex until Zuc hill, and that is the boundary running all the way around it, meaning this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So one more time, if you would, just so the Judges can orient themselves. I know it's difficult the way we're proceeding but if you could one more time take the pointer and pointed to the general area of the boundaries of the municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Here goes. Here, all the way down here. Let me just take a look. Here, here. To be precise, there's the river running along here. So that's where the boundary goes. This is where Dobrosevici and other neighbourhoods are and then it runs along the Miljacka river. Here it crosses this particular area, and here actually one part of this area belongs to Ilidza, the larger part of it. The Oslobodjenje part, which is now between the now-UN compound and Oslobodjenje. And then it runs along Nedzarici, over here, all the way here and it curves here, goes along the mountain passes and arrives here, and I don't know exactly the name of the street here. And then the entire left bank of Miljacka belongs to Novi Grad municipality, up until Otoka, and the right bank from the bridge onwards belongs to Novo Sarajevo, whereas Novi Grad is this area here, goes along the Zrak company and then down the slope towards the Bosna River and that's where it runs off. This is where the official airport is, Butmir, which belongs to Ilidza. It is just on the border, on the boundary opposite which is the Dobrinja neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cengic. Thank you, Madam Usher. Could I have the exhibit number of this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecution Exhibit P382.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if I could have the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we think it's already 284, this map. We think it's already in as 284.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I am not sure if 284 is not already marked. This is a blank map, as I said in my introduction for the purposes of future reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's continue. Mr. Registrar, could you find 284 for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the next exhibit, please, distributed. I assume, Mr. Registrar, this will be Prosecution Exhibit 383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's wait one second for the further numbering, Mr. Harmon, until we have clarified the first issue. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, the next exhibit in front of you is a census data taken from the 1991 census for the municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have that exhibit in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This exhibit shows, according to the Novi Grad 1991 census, that the total population of Novi Grad was 136.616 total population; the Muslims had 69.430; Serbs, 37.591; Croats, 8.869; Yugoslavs 15.580; and others, 5.126. Now, could you tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Cengic, what significant military and public facilities were located in the municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Let us start with the military facilities. The barracks which was called Viktor Bubanj barracks at the time, and the military court and the military prison contained within the former JNA barracks. Let me repeat. It was the barracks in the centre of the Novi Grad municipality; it was called Viktor Bubanj. And as far as I remember - I was not involved in politics before the war - there was also the military prosecutor's office, the military court and the military prison there. I'm not quite sure about the military prison, but it definitely was a military facility of the former JNA and it was called Viktor Bubanj before the war. The Halilovici barracks at Halilovici, and within the Rajlovac compound, there were barracks and military academy, also the factory of the aerial engines called Orao and military airfield called Rajlovac. The Nedzarici barracks at Nedzarici. Then the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina, large -- a large company called Zrak, which was a company of a semi-closed type, because it worked for the army. Then different factories of cables, reinforced material, the company Astro, and in the local community of Rajlovac, there was the main transformer station for the entire area of Sarajevo, also the main gas source for the entire Sarajevo, the main distribution centre for the entire town of Sarajevo and its environs. And I think I might have forgotten something there, but I do remember the main ones, in addition to the schools that were also there. But if necessary, I may enumerate them as well. For me, as a teacher, they are significant. For others, maybe they are not. There were 11 schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, was there a railroad depot and a railroad repair shop located in the Novi Grad municipality?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. In the Novi Grad municipality, there was the Alipasin Most station which was a freight station and that's where the railway depot was, where the repairs took place, and where the trains would be stored before being involved in traffic, before being operated. So that was the main hub there for the traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there also a water treatment plan and an oxygen factory located in the Novi Grad municipality?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: The oxygen factory was there, but not the water treatment. It was actually the town catchment for the treatment of waste water. But that wasn't the water used for drinking. Before the war, we used different springs for potable water, but the main source of it was at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. It was not the town catchment but the sewage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the municipality of Novi Grad also have major arterial routes that went toward Northern Bosnia running through them? I'm thinking particularly of the roads towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: There were two main roads leading out of the town, crossing the Novi Grad municipality. One of them went in the direction of Ilidza, leading onwards to Mostar and the sea; and the second road went across Rajlovac, in the direction of what is today the highway, and it was the main road leading to the north, towards Northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention, Mr. Cengic, on the multi-party elections in 1990 and I propose to lead you through this examination. I don't think the results what I'm going to be asking you about will be contested, unless counsel wishes to object, I propose to lead you with certain data and I'm going to ask you to affirm whether this is correct. During the 1990 multi-party elections, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ cooperated in order to defeat the Communist Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: At the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a sort of a partnership, relationship was established between these two parties, not a coalition, really, but somewhere in the vicinity of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the purpose of that coalition, if you say, cooperation was to defeat -- the communist parties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: At any rate, everyone has had enough of the 50 years of communist rule and this was one of the ways of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in the Novi Grad municipality, the results of those multi-party elections, in terms of party representation, and I won't name all of the parties, but were as follows: The SDA won 34 per cent of the vote; the SDS won 21 per cent of the vote; and the HDZ won 4 per cent of the vote. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in the Municipal Assembly of Novi Grad, there were 100 seats?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were elected by secret vote of the Municipal Assembly to the president, to the position of the president of the Municipal Assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it was a full-time job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, following the multi-party elections, how were the leading positions in the Novi Grad municipality distributed? How were decisions taken in respect of who, which party would represent -- would take which position? Can you explain that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: My first idea was that all the parties that won seats in the Assembly should be assigned part of the executive government as well. However, the SDS did not agree with that, with that proposal, since, at the level of the entire state, an agreement on partnership had been reached, then that opinion had to be honoured. So I gave up on that idea, to put through that kind of proposal, to include other parties that you did not mention here, and that is the SDP and the alliance of the reformist forces. So there was a division along the lines between the SDA, which had 36; the SDS [Realtime transcript read in error "SDA"], that had 21; and the HDZ, that had 4 seats. So if you look at the percentages involved and if you do the appropriate arithmetic, then there was a slightly different balance of power. According to this new mathematics, about 59 per cent was the SDA, and so on and so forth. It's not difficult to do the math involved. Negotiations went on, and like any negotiations, they were protracted. Of course, every party wanted to get as much as possible. To be quite frank, my intention was to have a division according to the results of the elections. I made an offer to Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik that he should give a proposal to see how things should be worked out. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 11, line 17, it seems that it says SDA where SDS is meant. In relation to 21. You see two times SDA appears, the second one should be SDS. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you: In terms of the negotiations between the parties, each party, and I'm talking now about the HDZ, the SDS, and the SDA, had negotiating teams that met and tried to agree on the distribution of positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And indeed, the negotiating team that represented the SDS included the - and let me just ask you to affirm this - Svetozar Milosevic, a member of the SDS who was elected president of the Executive Board of Novi Grad, Radislav Unkovic, who was the president of the Novi Grad municipality, Rade Novakovic, who was in the SDS, and Mr. Krajisnik; is that correct? Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: There is a mistake there. Unkovic was not president of the municipality. He was president of the SDS, Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Did I, in terms of identifying the negotiators for the SDS party, did I identify the four principal negotiators?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the negotiations for the SDA, there was yourself and Mr. Safet Hadzic, Mr. Muhamed Mrahorovic and Selim Jarkoc; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the HDZ had Mr. Jerkovic, Zeljko Jukic, and Darimir Curic [sic]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Curcic. Your pronunciation wasn't right. Jerkovic Ante, some of the first names are missing. Ante Jerkovic, Zeljko Jukic, Darimir Curcic. Now, that's the right name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of negotiating in the municipality of Novi Grad, for a municipal position, was Mr. Krajisnik elected to any particular position within the Novi Grad municipality?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: No. No. At that time, no one was elected to any position. The elections were simply over, and then Mr. Krajisnik was on the SDS list for the republican parliament, and I was on the SDA list for the municipal parliament. We knew that we had been elected, therefore, but nothing was done, I mean nothing more than that. This was the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the parties to the negotiations for these municipal-level positions were conducted by people who had been elected within the municipality, with the exception of Mr. Krajisnik, who had been elected to represent Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can put it this way: Negotiations mainly took place between and among the parties. Unkovic or Svetozar Milosevic or Novakovic were not elected to the Municipal Assembly. Mrahorovic was not on the SDA list for the Municipal Assembly either. Ante Jerkovic wasn't either. But these were the party delegations of the SDA, the HDZ and the SDS. So it was the party organs that were negotiating in order to set up a government. There were those who were elected in part at municipal level, and in part there were those who were at state level. Of course, every political party provided certain people from a certain area, probably the people that enjoyed the greatest degree of confidence. And therefore, the results were implemented in that way as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, the witness didn't quite answer Mr. Harmon's question, which Mr. Harmon probably noted and was maybe going to follow up anyway. But just a remark that the slightly leading form of the question, and I haven't objected to leading questions to bring out information fairly quickly on the basic stuff, but the slightly leading form of that question does appear to be inconsistent with something that we'd see in the witness's statement. So perhaps before Mr. Harmon does proceed, if he is going to proceed to try get an answer to the question that he asked, I might mention paragraph 11 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you're invited whenever you ask a witness something which seems not to be consistent with the statement not to lead if it's inconsistent -- well, at least if it's not exactly the same as what we find in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the end, Mr. Cengic, were the negotiations that your delegation had with the SDS delegation successful?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Well, they were. They were successful. We managed to sign an agreement and to distribute executive positions among these three parties, that is to say the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you inform the Court who the principal negotiator was on behalf of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether anyone had appointed them so, but three persons figured prominently in these talks. It so happened that on behalf of the SDA it was myself and then Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik on behalf of the SDS and Jukic on behalf of the HDZ. Now, whether this was official, whether this was the official position of the SDS, that's something I don't know. But at any rate, it is these three persons who had the main say in the negotiations: Myself, Mr. Krajisnik, and Mr. Jukic. Because what we would agree upon would be carried through ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us very succinctly what position the SDS took in respect of the positions that were subject to negotiations.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Well, at the first option that Mr. Krajisnik wanted was to get more than the election results would reflect. So we could not reach agreement straight away. Then what I proposed was that all the positions that are to be distributed should somehow be valued, with a certain number of points, and it is only that way that we could then distribute these positions. We could not distribute them on the basis of the numbers involved, because not all the positions are of equal importance in the municipality. Some position is more valid than two other positions. So I suggested that they be valued as double or more than double, and ultimately Mr. Krajisnik agreed to that. So every position had its own value. Then, on that basis, we carried out the distribution and we tried to match the election result in this effort too. However, at one point in time, Mr. Krajisnik made an offer. He said that he had agreed with Muhammed Cengic, who was then vice-president of the SDA, that the municipality of Novi Grad should get one more position than merited through the election results, and that this should be compensated for through the municipality of Cajnice. Since the municipality of Novi Grad at that time had about 100.000 voters at the time, and the municipality of Cajnice had about 3.000 voters, these two municipalities were not equal. One position in the municipality of Novi Grad had a large number of votes or voters behind it than the totality of the municipality of Cajnice. However, I said: Well, if that's the way it is, I'll go and check. So I had my doubts about this kind of agreement, but I decided to check it nevertheless. I made a different kind of offer, that the SDS -- or rather, the SDS should give the SDA one seat or one position as a compensation for Novi Grad, but in Banja Luka. Because at that time, the municipality of Novi Grad, in terms of its population figures, was close to the Banja Luka municipality. However, Mr. Krajisnik refused that. I checked at the SDA headquarters whether there was any such agreement with regard to this kind of an exchange of mandates, but they said that the answer was no, that no such agreement was reached. Then we went on. We looked at all the points, we did our math, in terms of all the positions involved, and in this way we distributed the executive and legislative branches of government in the territory of the municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: During the course of the negotiations, are you aware of whether Mr. Krajisnik consulted with others before arriving at decisions in respect of certain positions?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: These were indeed important decisions, because implementing the election results is a very important thing. Some things can be lost and some things can be gained through these negotiations. If negotiations are not conducted properly, some of the election results can even be lost in the process. Mr. Krajisnik would sometimes ask for a break and he'd go and consult someone. I had no need to take such breaks. The late Mr. Izetbegovic had full confidence in me, and I had full powers to decide in terms of what the most proper solution would be. Mr. Krajisnik nevertheless had to consult, but I did not find that to be anything unusual. The negotiations took place in the municipality building, where the offices of all the parliamentary parties are in the municipality of Novi Sad [as interpreted]. In hall 327, which is in the middle of the building, the SDA and the SDS and the HDZ had their offices on the first floor and they were right next door to each other. The communists gave us some small rooms, but nevertheless we managed to win the elections from there. There was only a wall separating the SDA offices from the SDS offices. Sometimes I would go to our rooms with my delegation, but more often we'd stay in the hall and wait for the SDS to return. When we went downstairs, I heard, on several occasions, that Mr. Krajisnik, since the walls are thin, talked to someone called Radovan or Raso. But I did not find that to be unusual. I was not eavesdropping. The wall was simply thin, and sometimes people speak very loud. So I did not really attach any importance to it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cengic, after the positions had been distributed, I want to focus your attention on a particular local commune of Rajlovac and a problem that developed within that local commune. First of all, can you tell the Judges what a local commune was and how many local communes there were within the Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: A local commune encompasses a certain area within the municipality of Novi Grad. Within Novi Grad there were 28 of them. This is a local community which, with the assistance of the municipality, resolves its own problems at this lower level. The problems that can resolve on its own, it resolves on its own, or they ask the municipality to resolve their problems at the level of the entire municipality. These problems pertain to the building of roads, to water supply, and other infrastructure. Then, when it is necessary to build new elementary schools and other things that are of vital importance within the local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, did each of these local communes have their own assemblies with elected members for those assemblies?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: This is the way it was: In view of the fact that in 1990 there were general elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the first free multi-party elections, that is, then the municipal organs were elected, the city organs, and the republican organs. In June and July, the term of office expired for the local commune agencies. They also had a four-year term. So the municipality of Novi Grad organised these local elections, if I can call them that, on the territory of the respective local communes. A professional in the local services who was in charge of setting the order of these citizens' meetings was Ms. Branka Vlahovic, a good lawyer, an ethnic Serb. She worked out the order for the citizens' meetings in local communes, and at every one of these meetings she was present too. Other persons from the executive and legislative branches, in order to assist the realisation of these meetings, went whenever Ms. Branka deemed it was necessary for them to go and attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we get too far ahead in the legislative developments in your municipality --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- is it correct that at these -- that each local commune at the meetings that you described elected their own representatives to represent the local commune?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: The citizens of the municipality from that local commune held citizens' meetings, and they were supposed to elect their own assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: So this meeting was where the electorate was represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to focus on the Rajlovac local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we could -- I'm fairly confident there isn't any doubt about it, but at page 18, line 19, where June and July was mentioned, it might be useful for the record to have it as 1991, which I'm perfectly confident it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In June and July the term of the office expired for the local commune agencies. That was your testimony, Mr. Cengic. I take it Mr. Stewart is correct; that's the year 1991. Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let us move on, focussing again on the Rajlovac local commune. I'm going to give you some statistics as to the ethnic breakdown of that commune and I'm going to ask you to affirm if this is correct. The total number of residents in that local commune was 4.013; there were 71 Croats, 1.160 Serbs, 2.618 Muslims, 134 persons who identified themselves as Yugoslavs, and 63 persons identified as "others"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik have his residence in the Rajlovac commune, specifically, in Zabrdje?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: He had a house in Zabrdje. He lived in Zabrdje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in 1991, was there a problem that arose in respect of the election of the Rajlovac representatives in that commune? You could just answer that question yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you had mentioned earlier in one of your answers that there were meetings that were scheduled in each of the local communes when the citizens of the local commune would get together and meet and elect representatives to their own local commune assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: The assembly and the other organs of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, July the 8th, 1991 was the date that was selected for the meeting when the citizens of the local commune of Rajlovac were to convene in order to conduct their elections; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you present at that meeting on July the 8th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Exactly at the time when the meeting was scheduled, that is to say, at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how many citizens from the local commune of Rajlovac were present at that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the meeting, there were 200 people, a bit over 200 people; but later on, more people came in, so there were a lot more than 200. Let's say that before the meeting actually started, we counted about 202 persons present, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were there people from all ethnicities present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you inform the Court what the problem was that developed at that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: It was customary for the representatives of the people to be present and for certain members to be proposed for the assembly. Bearing in mind that every part of the local commune should be represented in the assembly. Proposals for the assembly were made by Bosniaks and Croats. Mr. Boro Bjelica was present and he said that he is speaking on behalf of the Serbs and that they do not wish to attend the local commune meeting because they would establish a new local commune. That came as news to me. There was a bit of commotion. Serbs who did not belong to the SDS started complaining a bit: Who gave you the right to represent all Serbs? They were saying. But in order to pacify people, I said: All right. Tonight we are going to elect those that are not controversial. Next week we are going to have a meeting yet again. It was the list of the Bosniaks and the list of the Croats that were not controversial, and others too. I said: All right. Since the Serb side did not have a list, next week we will continue this meeting and then we are going to choose the representatives of the Serb people. In principle, we did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cengic, here, because I don't want to go to the meeting of the 16th of July. I want to stay in the meeting of the 8th of July. And let me ask you, first of all: Mr. Boro Bjelica, what party was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: He said that he was there on behalf of the SDS and that's why there was commotion, because those who were not members of the SDS approached him and said: Well, who gave you the right to speak on behalf of all of us? And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I take it from your testimony that there were some Serbs who were not members of the SDS who were present at that meeting who disagreed with the position taken by Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: They disagreed with his position and I believe that they were surprised at this position, Serbs and others, and that's when this commotion ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bjelica remain at that meeting after he made the announcement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Before he left, I told him if he could possibly confirm to me in writing what he had previously said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the meeting of July 8th, 1991, were candidates -- were lists of candidates put forward by the Serb members of the Rajlovac community and the Croat residents of that community?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: The lists were not complete yet because for them it was a whole new momentum. Generally there was this position that the entire territory of the local commune should be covered, so that the Serbs who were there and who were not members of the SDS, they were from different parts of the local commune. So that it was in their interest to create a comprehensive list so that each and every corner of the local commune would have its own representative at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I'd like you to listen very carefully to the question I ask. Now, at the end of -- by the end of the meeting on July the 8th, had there been selections made for Croat representatives and Muslim representatives for the Assembly of the local commune of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, because there was nothing controversial there. There were quite enough people there from the local commune so that they could vote and the lists were then compiled for the SDA, SDS, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the meeting to select the Serb representatives from the local commune of Rajlovac postponed until the 16th of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I was talking about one week, which meant that it was the 16th of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was there -- did you attend the meeting on the 16th of July, 1991? Yes, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Since this was a follow-up meeting on the first one, I felt the need to be there, although I did not have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could have the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the numbering of exhibits is concerned, although one could wonder whether it was necessary to tender another map next to P284, because 284 is almost exactly the same, but not for the full hundred per cent, we'll continue the numbering. That means that the new map now is P382, and then, Mr. Registrar, 383 is the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit P383 will be the 1991 consensus data for Bosnia, and Exhibit P384 will be the minutes of the meeting of the citizens of the local commune Rajlovac held on 16 July 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, do you have a copy, Mr. Cengic, of Prosecution Exhibit 384 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document that is dated in the upper left-hand corner the 22nd of July and this represents minutes of a meeting that took place at the Rajlovac local commune on the 16th of July, 1991 at 1800 hours, a meeting which you attended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like you to just direct your attention to the first list of ten names that appears. The first name is Milan. Do you see that list of names?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what that list represents.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: This is a list of Serbs from the territory of the Rajlovac local commune, from all the areas encompassed by the Rajlovac local commune, and this is a list of the Serbs who were to make up the Assembly of the Rajlovac local commune, in the order -- they are listed in the order according to the census for the population of that particular local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the week earlier, when Mr. Bjelica said that the Serbs were not going to participate in the election, nevertheless, the following week, these Serbs were put forward as candidates; correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs did put forth their candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were these Serbs, to your knowledge, any of these listed 1 through 10, members of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the conclusion of this particular meeting on the 16th of July, Mr. Cengic, were Serb representatives selected to the Assembly of the Rajlovac local commune?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. These same ten people listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we go down to the next lists, there are four lists in succession. Can you just tell the Court what those lists represent, and if there are any Serbs in each of those respective lists.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: With the election of the ten Serbs into the Assembly of the Rajlovac local commune, the assembly election procedure was completed. This was a sort of a legislative body at the local commune level, now the executive organs are ranked lower, and the main organ of the local commune is the local commune council, made up of ten members. You see here we have 11 members, and out of these 11, 6 are Bosniaks. Therefore, far less than those contained in the list. We were trying to achieve a compromise, and that's why Serbs were assigned more seats than originally planned by the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So in the second list, starting -- that has 11 names, are the last 4 names people who were Serbs, 8, 9, 10, and 11?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if you turn to the next list, the citizens who were proposed for members of the conciliation council, are numbers 4 and 5, to your knowledge, also Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I can merely assess that by their names. I did not ask them what ethnicity they belonged to. But yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And if you turn to the following list, the five persons' names, first being Nijaz, these were people who were unanimously elected to the supervisory board, were any Serbs in that particular list?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Number 5 -- that is, number 4 and number 5. As far as I can see, there were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And lastly, on the last list can you identify any Serbs in the consumer council?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Ranko Grujicic as far as I can see, under number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if we can turn to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P385.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which are excerpts from the minutes of the citizens meeting in Smiljevici held on the 2nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Cengic, is this -- when did you receive this document in respect of the meeting that was held on July 16th, 1991? Did you receive this document before or after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Together with the minutes of the meeting held on the 16th, or rather, when the elections were over, the Assembly of the Novi Grad municipality was supposed to verify the elections held in the local communes, and in that particular period, the results of all the elections that had taken place in all the parts of the municipality were being collected and this actually arrived together. It did not actually arrive directed to me but to the service of -- in charge of this particular local commune with the municipality. Because this particular service was supposed to submit a report to the Municipal Assembly on these elections that had been held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. We're getting slightly confused here by this. The question that was put at page 26, line 24, 25, this document, Mr. Cengic, is this: "When did you receive this document in respect to the meeting that was held on July 16th, 1991?" Maybe I'm just misunderstanding. The document we've just been handed relates to a meeting held on the 2nd of July. But I'm not sure whether Mr. Harmon's meaning to link this document with the meeting on the 16th of July. That may be the explanation. But in that case, I'm still unclear as to what this link is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can say, Your Honour, that this document, this dated -- obviously relates to a meeting on the 2nd of July. My question to Mr. Cengic was when did he see this document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In that case, I don't really understand why the meeting of the 16th of July was referred to in the question. That's what confused me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand that it was only after the meeting of the 16th was held that Mr. Cengic received this. Because when you receive the minutes of a meeting it's usually after the meeting. So that it's more than two weeks or more later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: These are minutes of a meeting held on the 2nd of July. That's my whole point, Your Honour. I don't understand why the meeting of the 16th of July was referred to in the question at all and why the witness wasn't just asked when he received this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Because I'm trying to put a date that's important in relation to when he received this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Why doesn't Mr. Harmon simply ask him first of all when he received the document and then proceed from that simple question and answer to where we go next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the questions could have been put in a different way, but it does not confuse me, and it doesn't confuse the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. Perhaps I'm the only one that's confused. We have the slight disadvantage with this document, supplied with B/C/S, but the English version of this is something we've only just seen this second. But I -- my confusion was really perhaps in the end not understanding why the -- there was any mention -- I suppose there was some reason for the 16th of July meeting being mentioned in the question at all. But it doesn't seem there was a good reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether there was a good reason or not, it doesn't confuse us and I do not think that -- the Chamber doesn't think that it's inadmissible to put a question in this way to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not confused any more, Your Honour. I'm not happy, but I'm not confused any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just check to see when the English version of this document was given to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed at this moment, since Mr. Stewart is not confused any more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, let me direct your attention first of all to the first paragraph in this document. This document -- have you had a chance to --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Could I please get the B/C/S version, the Bosnian version, if you have one. If not, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, is the B/C/S version not -- the last couple of pages of the same document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Could we have this in the Bosnian, this on the screen. No? Okay. Then fine; we can proceed. We can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, if we look at this document, this document in the first paragraph says a large number of citizens, 100, a representative of the Novi Grad municipality and an employee of the Rajlovac local commune were present at the meeting. And in this particular document, under sub-part 2, these 100 citizens were informed by Mr. Boro Bjelica about an initiative to establish the local commune of Zabrdje after separation from the present local commune. And it lists a group of four people who were appointed to prepare and submit to the Novi Grad municipality a request for separation. At the end of this document, Mr. Cengic, it says: "Around 400 signatures in support of this position were collected previously." Last line for the signature. Did you ever see that petition with 400 signatures?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: No. I did not even see it, let alone receive a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I clarify. I should say straight away. My apologies. We had received this document in English before. As a team here we were slightly confused because Ms. Cmeric had received an e-mail with only the B/C/S attachment, so she'd not seen the English and informed me -- but in fact we have got it. So I acknowledge it was not the first time we received the English version in the last few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Stewart, I'm trying to make this not only today but the whole of the trial, as smooth as possible. And since I stopped Mr. Harmon when he wanted to explain when exactly he provided that to you, because I thought at that moment it would not make that much difference, then I think it -- I stopped him really and I think then to clarify issues that are not at that moment very important, I could have imagined that you would not have responded to what I prevented Mr. Harmon to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm terribly sorry, but in fact the reason I intervened was first of all to offer an apology to Mr. Harmon, and secondly because I understood that Mr. Harmon and his team might have wasted time and energy, as Mr. Harmon was offering to do, finding out when they first gave us the document and I wanted to save them the effort of doing that when I could immediately see that I got it wrong. I believe it was entirely appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stopped him already at that time to do that in open court, of course, whatever- --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But he would have done it behind the scenes. I wanted to stop the Prosecution, because they're great friends of mine, Your Honour, I wanted to stop them from doing unnecessary work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say develop your friendly relationship to the extent necessary in court and to the extent not necessary, outside of court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the next exhibit, please, which will be a map and which will be Exhibit 386. This exhibit, Your Honours, is a map and a legend which I have prepared with the assistance of Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, when you examine this exhibit and can you confirm that at my request you prepared a map that related to, first of all, marked in green are the approximate boundary line of part of the Novi Grad municipality, the pink line represents the approximate boundary line of the Rajlovac local commune, and the blue line represents the approximate boundary line of the proposed new local commune of Zabrdje. Did you prepare this map and is that correct what I have said?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I drew this on the basis of my memory as to the situation with regard to the municipality, so I do note that there may be some errors, but not significant ones. As for the blue line, that's based on my assumption on what the request was, because I never received an official map representing the local commune that was supposed to be established by the Serbs. Therefore, this blue line was drawn on the basis of an assumption. I don't have any valid proof of that because I did not receive any. But that's what I inferred on the basis of their requests and on the basis of their proposal, although at a later stage I did say that for practical reasons, it would have been a good idea to provide us with the map. Because whatever ideas we had for the municipality, we put them down on the map. We would -- we knew exactly which house belonged to which local commune. However, the proposing party did not accommodate my request. So this blue-lined map is something I drew on the basis of my assumption of what their proposal had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Within the blue line, there are seven dots, numbered 1 through 7. And did you assist me by identifying each particular relevant feature in respect of each numbered dot?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Harmon wants to lead through this, because he's very helpfully supplied me with a list, so if it speeds things up, I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would ask the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to tender the legend as well with the map. I just want to get his answer as to whether he assisted me in terms of identifying those features and placing those dots on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that you're asking what he did and not -- yes. Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, did you assist me in identifying the features and did we mark those features with numbers 1 through 7?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, on the basis of what I remembered, given the time that elapsed. I might have made a mistake with the figure somewhere, but these features were indeed on that particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I would have one question, because under number 7, railroad depot, railroad repair shop appears, Mr. Cengic. Your earlier testimony was that there was a railroad depot, railroad repair in Alipasin Most. Is that the same? Because at least number 7 appears closer to Rajlovac than Alipasin Most. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's where the freight station was. At Alipasin Most, there was this smaller station, but this more important depot was situated where number 7 is. Because before the war, I taught as a teacher at a railway school and I took my students there quite often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you'll see, Your Honour, it's difficult to put a number to cover the whole feature. There's a series of parallel lines, which is essentially a series of railroad lines and it's the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that this legend was probably prepared fairly recently. Do I take it that there isn't a B/C/S version of this piece of paper with the seven points at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is not. We just prepared this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The only reason I ask is because I understand the witness is confirming that he helped prepare it, so it was done in English, but that means, of course, Mr. Krajisnik doesn't have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would there be a possibility -- I take it that translation will be made on very short notice and that perhaps meanwhile Ms. Cmeric could assist in the accused to understand what is this perhaps during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I was only really trying this week to relieve Ms. Cmeric of an extra task of translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will be glad to provide one, Your Honour. We'll get one before the conclusion of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cengic, you were confronted with a demand, essentially, to create a new municipality, local commune of Zabrdje, out of a community, local commune of Rajlovac. What did you do, what steps did you take, to solve the problem?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, I was opposed to any sort of divisions at any level. Probably I was guided by what I knew of the war in Croatia, and this frightened me in a way, and that's why I took a pragmatic position of trying to solve problems. In view of the fact that I did not see the list that was mentioned here, this petition signed by 400 persons for the separation of the local commune, I really had my great suspicions about the very existence of this document. That's why I asked for a survey to be conducted on the ground, amongst the populace that was enveloped by the particular local commune that was supposed to become a local commune on the request of the Serbs, without actually knowing that I was going to need this at a certain point. And when I started writing a book, I managed to save some of these documents and among them were lists produced by this survey, just an incomplete record, because I was unable to have the files of these. Because the person who was in charge of the archives, who we usually called such a person "secretary," he took away both the stamp and the whole documentation. He was the -- Zeljko Travar, members of the SDS. However, I did find some traces of it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt again and ask you to listen very carefully to the question I'm asking. The question I asked was what did you do and you started to describe a survey. Can you tell the Court how that survey was conducted.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I didn't do this myself. It's citizens of the local commune of Rajlovac who went from one house to another, in different areas, in Smiljevici, Zabrdje, Dvor, then the Franjo Kluz neighbourhood, et cetera, and they asked citizens whether -- or actually, I didn't want to put a leading question in any way. I actually phrased the question in a way which was unfavourable to me. I don't have it here right now, but it is written down. This question that was put to the citizens was not one that favoured me. It was actually the opposite. So I would appreciate it if it could be read out, because I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I'm going to supply you with a copy of the next exhibit. It's 387. And I'm going to ask you to identify these exhibits. It's an exhibit of three pages.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: What I wished to point out here is that every list has, at the very beginning, the following wording: We, the below-mentioned citizens are in favour of leaving the local commune. So I did not suggest an answer that would favour my own opinion. I put one that was the other way around. And then we have a list of citizens, their names and surnames, and their signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we take a look at the survey from the area 21 May street, Rajlovac, it's in the upper left-hand corner, we see a list with 35 names and we have a yes, and a no column. And I take it, Mr. Cengic, if you answered no, you were not in favour of separation from the Rajlovac local commune; and if your answer was yes, then you were in favour of separation from the local commune. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: You're right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the list for the people surveyed from the area of 21 May Street Rajlovac, the last six names, those people indicated they were in favour of leaving; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we turn to the survey form for the Smiljevici settlement, we see the responses were all in the negative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we turn to the area of Franjo Kluz, we see that there were three abstentions and the remaining people in that particular area were opposed to the separation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, are these -- this exhibit is an example, are examples of the form -- the survey forms that were used; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: These do not represent the total results of the survey that was conducted in the Rajlovac local commune; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: This may be considered a random sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as a result of conducting the survey of the residents in the Rajlovac local commune, do you recall what the results were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before we continue, I see that in the translation, the question put on the top of the answers is always translated in exactly the same way. At the same time, I see that at least, apart from talking about being confused, whether confusion could be -- could arise from this question. But I see that in the original, the words are at least not exactly the same. And I'd like first to check. And I'll just draw your attention to the detail, for example, that in the first one, the 21st of May Street, at least I identify a word which reads like "Potpisani" which, as far as I can see, does not appear in the second page with the question and does appear again on the third page. I'm not saying that it's incorrectly translated, but at least I'd like to be sure that what is translated as literally the same question is -- does reflect the two versions of the question as they appear on top of the B/C/S lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. These are official translations. I don't read the language. So if we could perhaps ask Mr. Cengic to read the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, if you could read --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Obviously they are the same. However, some copies are illegible, because it is a poor copy, you see. But yes, what it says here is the same thing. The text is the same. We, the undersigned --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you would just listen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I see at least one word what does not appear in one of the questions. Could you perhaps, because that's I think the -- these are the copies best readable, first read the question as it exactly appears in the B/C/S version of the document which is about the Smiljevici settlement, that is, the -- in B/C/S, it's the second page, and the last three digits on the top stamped on that page are 456. Could you please slowly read the text of that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We, the below-mentioned citizens, are in favour of leaving the local commune." And now the question reads as follows: "We are not in favour of leaving." The content is the same, except that the letters are small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I'm not asking for comment. I just asked you to read --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me. It could be, I hesitate, but it could be that we could shorten things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. On the Defence side, Your Honour, we're quite satisfied that the distinction is an immaterial distinction between something that means undersigned and something that means below stated, and the substance is exactly the same. And if the Prosecution are happy, we are happy that there is no material distinction here at all and that there's no need to explore this translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for your assistance please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see what you meant. I did not quite understand at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the results of the survey that was conducted in the Rajlovac local commune showed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: The majority was against the separation, against the local commune leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in July of 1991, in an attempt to resolve this problem that had developed in the Rajlovac local commune, did you call Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik to assist you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Before that, I sent letters to all the major companies that we identified here a few minutes ago. About 10.000 workers were employed there. And I asked them for their opinions and I got a negative answer on that score. Then I -- or actually, we have to bear in mind the following: August is a time when people go on vacation usually. That's a month when people usually go on vacation. So I asked Mr. Krajisnik to come and to help me resolve this problem. Because he was very influential and that he lived there -- or rather, I don't know whether he lived there. I don't know whether he lived there when he was an elected official, but I knew that his parents lived there and that his parents' house was there and I knew that he was influential in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he respond to your request?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Well, my understanding was that Mr. Krajisnik was very busy during those days, but he did come, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting with him to try to resolve the problem that was confronting you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges that meeting.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik came to my office. It was on the first floor. We had a cup of coffee there. And then I started describing the problem. I realised that Mr. Krajisnik was aware of the problem, had been aware of the problem, and in a way he supported the sponsors of that proposal. We did not talk about it that much. Mr. Krajisnik dealt with his own problem to a greater extent. He asked for someone to come from the town planning office so that he could figure out how he would legalise his house. I had invited him to resolve the problem at hand, and Mr. Krajisnik moved on to finding a solution to his own personal problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say in your answer: "And in a way he supported the sponsors of the proposal," can you be more explicit in how he expressed that to you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to remember after 15 years what his words were. I do not remember exactly, but the gist of the wording more or less coincided with the tone of the letter sent by Boro Bjelica. I cannot remember the words now, after 15 years. At that time -- well, words did not mean a great deal to me. They did not lead to a solution to the problem. Because we still had a status quo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, at the time you had this meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, had you received the results of the survey that we discussed that was conducted?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could have the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before we continue, I look at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm happy to take a break at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this point in time. Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we distribute this exhibit or we could distribute it and then we could--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could distribute the exhibit and then ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P388, Your Honours, that's the article "What to do with Zabrdje" by Ankica Posavljak for the Novogradsko Oko, first issue Sarajevo, February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to appear, Your Honour, the legend for the map has been prepared. I've distributed it to counsel. It's been hopefully distributed to Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. As a matter of fact, I reread the answer of the witness in relation to the railway depot, et cetera. It was not quite clear whether he at that time already referred to this railway complex or to the railway complex which is quite nearby. But I think at this moment it's not something vital. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could -- then the last exhibit has been distributed, I take it. It's Prosecution Exhibit 388. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, in front of you is a Prosecution exhibit. It is a translation of an article. It is headed "What to do with Zabrdje?" Let me first of all put this article in the right context. This article appeared in a publication Novogradsko Oko, printed in Sarajevo in February of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And as to this interview that we're going to be paying attention to, interview of Mr. Krajisnik, we don't know when exactly this interview took place, based on what's contained in the newspaper article; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to parts of this article. You testified earlier that you had asked Mr. Krajisnik to come to Novi Grad to assist in the dispute over the settlement, the new settlement of Zabrdje. Let me read to you a portion of this article and interview with Mr. Krajisnik. I'm referring to the last paragraph in the English translation of page 1: "I promised to Ismet Cengic that I would do everything to prevent the use of violence and to make sure that changes are carried out as determined by the constitution and according to the decision of the Municipality. However, the Municipality made mistake because this issue was not included in the Assembly agenda and they did not meet natural request of the citizens, even though all inhabitants of this area came out in favour of establishing local commune." Now, I'd like to ask you, Mr. Cengic: In your meetings with the Serb representatives, local representatives, prior to your meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, had there been any threats of violence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: There weren't. This is the first time this became part of the dialogue, this violence. I don't know why. No one ever mentioned violence before in any talks. This is the first time it appeared officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, is the portion of the interview where Mr. Krajisnik says: "All of the inhabitants of this area came out in favour of establishing a local commune" based on the information that was available to you on the 8th of July and based on the information that subsequently you became aware of from the survey? Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Obviously, this is not correct, even if the poll had not been carried out, the one that I had initiated, 400 signatories does not include all the inhabitants of the local commune, if you look at the census, you will see that this does not constitute a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cengic, you've described your efforts to resolve the problem, first of all by conducting a survey to verify yourself what the popular will was; two, calling Mr. Krajisnik. You also created a commission to look into this problem; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that all the steps that I had taken had not yielded results, I proposed to all political parties that they all appoint a representative each, and that we should tour the area and see whether we can find a solution to the problem. The delegation consisted of all the parliamentary parties in the Municipal Assembly of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did that commission yield results that helped you solve the problem or was it unsuccessful?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. No. Nothing happened. Quite simply, the sponsors of the proposal were not in favour of a debate. They wanted to have a local commune of their own and they did not let the commission have proper insight, except for a rough map of the local commune, and they did not even give them a more detailed explanation. They did not even give them a study on the matter involved or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to now go to the next exhibit, which is a binder, Your Honours. It contains 11 intercepts and it contains also a declaration prepared by the witness. This will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 389. To orient Your Honours to this exhibit, you will see there are tabs between each of these exhibits. They bear a KID number and a tab number, and I will be referring to -- will be playing four intercepts out of this and I'll direct Your Honours to the appropriate tab number for the text of the intercept. Mr. Cengic, in respect of this particular exhibit, did you have the opportunity to listen to a number of exhibits -- number of intercepts in the last two days?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were you asked to identify or attempt to identify the voices contained in those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In most cases, I managed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if you would take a look at -- in the binder itself, you'll see a declaration and two pages attached to that declaration. Do you see that part of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I recognised these.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And does this declaration that says that you have listened to the following intercepted telephone conversations and identified voices of the participants as indicated below, does this declaration bear your signature and the date of November 6th, 2004?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the second and third pages of this declaration, do your initials -- does your signature appear in the lower right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: My initials, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
