utterances.text: And in the actual pages 2 and 3 of the declaration, if you turn to that, you will see a section that deals with voice ID, and as to each particular intercept, have you identified by name those persons whose voices you recognised in the specific intercept?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I recognised all the ones that are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. If we could turn to the intercept, Your Honours, this is an intercept, and counsel, this is an intercept that is found at tab 4 of the exhibit 389. If we could play that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the text been provided to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be translated into French for the completeness of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It has, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I was down in Novi Grad until late. I couldn't make -- Radovan KARADZIC: Well, how is it down there? What's the situation? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, you know, the assembly is. Radovan KARADZIC: Blocked. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Outvoting completely blocked. Radovan KARADZIC: Right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: So we agreed on something. They wanted it immediately. You know what our people are like, so --. Radovan KARADZIC: Yeah, yeah. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: So we have made a different arrangement. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I calmed down things a bit. They are -- they never -- I remember when I was -- well, there was a split later. That man Unkovic contributed a lot to that, but there were others as well. Radovan KARADZIC: I told you, man, that is -- he is privately -- he appears to be good and --. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes. You are -- well, you were completely right. Radovan KARADZIC: No, they are. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I have to -- Radovan KARADZIC: Well, you know, they are unsuitable personalities. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's right, quarrelsome. Well, not quarrelsome. There are various --. Radovan KARADZIC: Intolerant, hard. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: It's a bit of a problem, but that, all in all, let me tell you -- Radovan KARADZIC: They are not open to others, you know. He can't take on board any new position which he likes, which he might like, somebody else's position. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: They are deficient personalities, and he remains narrow-minded. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Only broad-minded personalities can -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: To take on board, to enrich themselves. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: With other peoples' positions, which become theirs. You know that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes, you're right. Radovan KARADZIC: He can't do that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Where are you now? Radovan KARADZIC: At the clinic. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That thing yesterday, how did you fare up there in that respect? Radovan KARADZIC: Oh, fine. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah? Radovan KARADZIC: I see lots of publicity. Only Oslobodjenje doesn't give a word about it, but on all the front pages, in Borba, everywhere. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Right, it's a disgrace now they're doing this. It's -- Radovan KARADZIC: A disgrace, a disgrace, but there's no -- well, they will wake up one day. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Right. Radovan KARADZIC: On another topic, there is a small disappointment. You will understand me. It appears that Milosevic, he went to Macedonia. It seems that he made a step in the direction of Izetbegovic's platform. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: And fuck -- in this internal -- you understand me completely, don't you? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I know, I know. With them? Radovan KARADZIC: No. Both with them and for them and for Bosnia. Well, he says you and Bosnia determine -- arrange your relations as you see fit, but some mutual sovereignty could be -- you could guarantee it to each other, something like that. To tell you the truth, simply put, I was disappointed. He went down for negotiations for talks with this Gligorov. I don't know whether they will issue a statement or not regarding this. But, you know, fuck. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. With him down there, but with this one over there? Radovan KARADZIC: Well, I think he is evidently -- if not that, I think it was suggested to him by the Americans, the English, and the French. If they will not accept that, then they are fucked. Alija, you know, they had it up to here with Alija and with Gligorov. Gligorov also cannot, won't. America won't quarrel with Greece over Gligorov. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. Radovan KARADZIC: It will not quarrel with Greece, so they are ready for consultation. Here you have a smaller Yugoslavia with a condition that the republics internally should be sovereign in relation to each other. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. Radovan KARADZIC: Some kind of internal sovereignty, that is, the sovereignty be tied to the citizens, peoples and republics, so that that is understood. But of course, the citizens and the peoples. However, there is no way we can agree to this. I don't know now how we are going to enter into a conflict with Milosevic now? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No problem. Easy. Radovan KARADZIC: We'll have to enter into a conflict with Milosevic now. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, no. We'll do it nicely. Don't worry. Radovan KARADZIC: I don't know. He is -- well, because if Alija - Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Have you seen him? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. You know, when the two of us think the same. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: You and I think the same when we speak and everything. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Well now, I was looking at that draft and all that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Um, is it any good? Radovan KARADZIC: Well, no, insofar as it is a step towards --. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, I know. Radovan KARADZIC: Towards that platform. But I realise that actually they told him the foreign factor advised him that Serbia should make that concession and that if Izetbegovic and Gligorov did not accept it, then Gligorov would be finished, because Greece would not -- America would not sacrifice Greece, which is very important to them down there in the Mediterranean. Macedonia would not get any kind of independence. Izetbegovic would also get a rap on the knuckles, because if he should refuse that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah, he will not refuse. Radovan KARADZIC: I'm afraid he will not refuse. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Only maybe these other ones will not refuse, but -- Radovan KARADZIC: I am afraid they will not refuse, because a great concession for him. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, no. Radovan KARADZIC: The sovereignty should be tied to the republic as well as the citizens, peoples, and republics. Should be tied to the republic, that is very suspicious, because that's a way out for him. He will endorse this with open arms, because that's basically a return to his position. And if he should refuse, then we would be sitting pretty. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He won't refuse, no way. Radovan KARADZIC: If he should refuse, then -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He won't. Radovan KARADZIC: Then we would be sitting pretty. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Just a little bit more than he's got, that's excellent for him. Radovan KARADZIC: Yeah. I don't know. If he should refuse, because then we would have -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Let's not worry. We'll see. Let it run its course. We have -- Radovan KARADZIC: I'm fucking worried. We would have to go openly with -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, no. We'll find a way out, don't you worry. Radovan KARADZIC: How will you find a way out if he agrees to it? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We'll do our work, don't you worry. Radovan KARADZIC: Because look -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Inside that, firm. Radovan KARADZIC: Yeah, if he should agree. If he agrees, then you cannot, then you can't, then the foreigners will put pressure on us. If he should refuse, then everybody, then our actions are fully justified, 100 per cent justified. I think not -- regionalisation is not the problem now in terms of the internal organisation of the republic, but -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I know. Radovan KARADZIC: Our problems, our plans then fall through. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I know. Radovan KARADZIC: Because they will say to you: What do you want? Bosnia has agreed to the organisation of the state. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: If he has sovereignty in relation to Serbia and to others, that is mutually -- if they are -- if they guarantee sovereignty, that's a big problem now, you know, because the world wants to preserve the Yugoslav framework, but not as a communist creation but as a democratic Yugoslavia. They want -- these foreigners want Bosnia not to be Islamic, not to get an Islamic republic. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes. Radovan KARADZIC: And I can tell you that I was terribly disappointed. This about Yugoslavia is excellent, but I was disappointed by Milosevic making this step in the direction of Izetbegovic and Gligorov. However, I got the impression I could not discuss it fully, openly, because I got the impression that this was suggested to him by the English, the French, and the Americans, to make this concession. So that if they refuse, then they are fucked. If they refuse and if Croatia refuses the Blue Helmets, then it is fucked. Babic is full of shit. We will have to put the squeeze on him. We shall write to his people down there that he is steering a dangerous course. Vance's must be accepted down there, not for Bosnia, but down there it must. There you are now. Now you think about it, I think you understood me completely. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Completely, completely. Radovan KARADZIC: You completely understood my concerns. I mean, fuck, you bleed, you work on something for a year and a half, and then at one point he makes a concession like that. I understand that there is pressure and that that is politics and that it is pressure for the foreign powers. I think that right now America, England and France are in control of the game because they want to put Germany in a tight spot. Yup. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: But we must not rely on that, somebody not doing something. We must know what we want. Radovan KARADZIC: No, but the problem is, what if he accepts? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well he's sure to accept. Both of them are. Neither of them has a way out. Radovan KARADZIC: I know, but fuck, then that is inconvenient for us. I know. That's the problem. Radovan KARADZIC: Because he accepted them; he sold his skin dear. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: He sold his skin dear and -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Huh. Radovan KARADZIC: That is the domination in Yugoslavia and Bosnia. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah, sure. Radovan KARADZIC: In Bosnia itself and in Yugoslavia. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: What's the matter with you? Do you realise what that means? Oh, dear. Radovan KARADZIC: I don't know. We shall have to pursue our own policy. We'll have to pursue our own policy, even at the price of splitting with Milosevic. I don't think we have -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Tell me, are you planning for the two of us to sit down for a while? Radovan KARADZIC: We would have to. I heard that we're thinking about something tomorrow. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No. Radovan KARADZIC: Milan told me, something having to do with businessmen. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, I told them something else. I was thinking that we should sit down a bit today. Radovan KARADZIC: All right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We had a meeting here yesterday. I don't think we are planning to go. I have a meeting here. Radovan KARADZIC: When is that? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well I don't know. We can -- you and I can sit down here. You can have a rest. After four or five hours. All right? Radovan KARADZIC: All right. That's fine. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right, we'll talk again later. Radovan KARADZIC: All right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I'll think it over."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, this is an intercept that was recorded on the 26th of December, 1991, in which Mr. Krajisnik, on page 1 of the English version, translation, says that he had been down in Novi Grad until late. Now, I'd like to turn to the next exhibits, two exhibits, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar, if we could take and give the number 390 to the document that bears the ERN number 00707977. And if we could give the exhibit number 391 to the exhibit that bears the ERN number 00707976, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those two documents are numbered accordingly, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if the witness could be given both of those exhibits at the same time, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, these documents have now been distributed. Let me direct your attention to both of these exhibits. I know you're familiar with them. If you could turn your attention first of all to Exhibit 390, and this is an exhibit that is a letter that is addressed to you. On the second page, it bears the date 27 of December, 1991. And I want to ask you just very quickly about some features in that letter. First of all, can you identify any of the signatures that appear at the end of that letter under the caption "Municipal SDS board, Club of Representatives"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Mijatovic, president of the Club of Representatives of the Municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cengic, on that same document there is handwritten item on the first page above the addressee. It says "30/12/1991." Do you see what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know whose signature, whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I used to date the documentation upon receiving it, so that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in this particular letter, this letter is essentially a letter of complaint, and it identifies, in part, the basis of the complaint, and I'm quoting from the last paragraph on page 1 of the English: "The failure to put on the agenda the citizens' initiative to separate and establish the local commune of Rajlovac 1." On the second page of the English translation, the last paragraph, it reads: "If you choose to maintain the present situation, we would like to inform you that our people, in order to protect their national interests, will establish their own Serbian Assembly and will exclusively implement and observe its decisions." Now, would you compare this document with then Prosecutor's Exhibit 391, the next exhibit, which is an exhibit which, as one can see at the bottom of the text, has -- bears the date 23 December 1991, and it is a -- the subject is a proposal for the impeachment of the president of the Novi Grad Sarajevo Municipal Assembly. Let me direct your attention to two features on this letter. First of all, there is a stamp on the upper right-hand side of this document that says "Received 27 December 1991." Is that the date when this document was received by the Novi Grad Sarajevo Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the official stamp of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the document, there is handwriting with a signature. Is that your signature? It says "received on 31 December."

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Just to put these in the proper chronological order: Which of these two documents, 390 or 391, did you receive first?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: The one with it says "30th December 1991" on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that's Prosecution Exhibit 390 you received first?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, despite your efforts to resolve the situation in respect to the Rajlovac new local commune, was that problem effectively resolved?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: It was not resolved. The SDS was well aware of it not having been solved and that it was impossible to solve it, because the Municipal Assembly had not officially received the documentation it had asked for, that is to say, the map, and the explanation backing the request for the separation. Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this letter does not bear the municipal stamp on the top. This document, therefore, did not go through the regular procedure but was handed in directly to me by a person who was a representative of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Cengic, "this document," are you referring to Prosecution Exhibit 390 or Prosecution Exhibit 391?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: This letter containing the reasons, without a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That would be Prosecution Exhibit 390; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I don't have that one here. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm mistaken on that. You have -- you should have two documents in front of you, Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One is a document that is numbered 391, one is a document that is numbered 390. Perhaps the usher can assist the witness in identifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, the document with the list of 20 signatures is P3 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where? Where does it say that? I don't see that any -- written anywhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me assist you a different way, Mr. Cengic. Apparently the number is not indicated on that particular document. 391 bears the ERN number at the top --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if the witness would look at the original, then we have a clear distinction. 391, half of the page is covered with 20 signatures. That's the document we're looking at, at this moment. Could you please -- the original B/C/S, could you just show it -- that's the one we have, yes. That's 391. Please concentrate on that one. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said in your testimony, Mr. Cengic, one of these documents was not received in the regular course of business. Which document was not received in the regular course of business? The one with the 20 signatures or --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: The other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That would be 390, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is 390, the one with the stamp and two signatures at the bottom dated 27th of December, 1991. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, very quickly, Mr. Cengic, in respect of Prosecution Exhibit 391, the proposal to impeach you, were you impeached?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the next intercept, if we can. This is the intercept that is found, Your Honours, at tab 7. It is an intercept --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we turn to the next intercept, we observe that there wasn't a single question apparently asked in relation to the previous intercept. It was played for about five minutes and we were not aware that any question was actually put to the witness. So we're wondering what the precise purpose is or justification for playing intercepts if a question is not actually going then to be addressed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my response is this: This intercept that we just played is dated -- was dated December 26th. It is an intercept that Mr. Krajisnik says he had been down in Novi Grad all night. He refers to problems. We have two letters at or about the same time that come to Mr. Cengic, one of which complains, and there is a threat to establish their own Serbian municipality. The other is a document that threatens to impeach Mr. Cengic. The Court obviously can make whatever inferences it wishes from those three exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we still don't quite follow. The witness wasn't a party to the conversation that the intercept represents. It's, in a sense, nothing then to do with him directly. He's not asked any questions at all about it. It's got, in a sense, nothing to do with this witness. We've indicated before that we, if invited to agree that it's Mr. Krajisnik's voice on a tape and somebody else's voice on a tape, we probably wouldn't have any major difficulty with that. And then intercepts of genuine conversations speak for themselves. But if no question at all is going to be addressed to a witness there is no justification for introducing it in the course of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber considers it in the following way: This is an intercept, one among more intercepts, in relation to which the witness has identified at least many speakers, not all of them, but at least in each conversation one or more of the speakers. The Chamber understands the playing of the intercept on which the voices of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic have been identified by the witness, the playing of this intercept for a better understanding of the Chamber of other documents that are tendered by Mr. Harmon does more or less emphasise the importance of this intercept, of this telephone conversation, in relation to the developments in the local commune of Rajlovac. And the Chamber thinks -- is of the opinion that this is admissable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we then make a supplementary observation that we still raise the question whether it's necessary to play the whole of this intercept which went on way beyond the linking point that Mr. Harmon sought to establish. With this additional observation, Your Honour, that so far as any value of the transcript in English and French appearing, so far as that value is concerned, it's seriously diminished by the almost incomprehensibility of the text on the transcript because it doesn't break it up between one speaker and another. There's just a continuous run on the transcript. So that's of no real value. So we do question -- it's virtually incomprehensible, Your Honour, when one reads the transcript in English and I assume that French speakers, although at least as intelligent as English speakers would still have the same difficulty. So, Your Honour, we really question the value of playing pages and pages and pages or minutes and minutes and minutes of a tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me respond to that. Because this intercept more specifically deals with what this witness, his testimony about the Rajlovac commune. But let me answer Mr. Stewart. Because in part of the indictment, as Your Honours are aware, we -- one of the portions of the allegation are there was a close relationship between the two and because of those associations, there was certain power to Mr. Krajisnik. Specifically, on page 4 of the English transcript of this indictment [sic], there is evidence that's relevant to that as well. And I'm referring to Mr. Karadzic, where he says: "Yes, yes, you know when the two of us think the same." Krajisnik says: "Yes." Karadzic says: "You and I think the same when we speak and everything." And Krajisnik says: "Yes." So there are other portions of this intercept that I think it is important for the Court to hear. I think it's important for the Court to hear the voices, the relationship, the tone between these two people. More specifically, this witness, and my concern with this witness dealt with the portions of it that are on page 1 that dealt with Mr. Krajisnik being in Novi Grad at or about the time these letters are received. But I think these -- playing these intercepts in their totality, a selected number of them, is important for the Court because the Court can get information that also relates to other parts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you'd say part of the intercept, not indictment, as you said, I think, but part of the intercept is of direct relevance for the testimony of this witness, whereas other parts, you play them in order to draw the attention of the Court on those parts of a conversation of -- that, according to this witness, has been a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that sort of answers the question, because our question, which was really what's a lot of this got to do with this particular witness. The answer seems to be clear, absolutely nothing at all. If it's being frankly said, well, it hasn't got anything to do with this witness but we'd just like at this point to play it to the Trial Chamber and put it in evidence for what it's worth, then at least we understand what's going on. But let's not delude ourselves that most of it has got anything to do with the particular witness. And we've had this many, many times in the course of this case. We then raise the question, Your Honour, whether it would be better if the Prosecution want to put a whole lot of transcripts before the Trial Chamber for its information if it was done in a way that made them -- made them comprehensible to any later reader of the transcript. Because what anybody reading the transcript in future is going to have to find the original transcript of the conversation in order to make any sense at all of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, what makes sense and what makes not sense sometimes is only to be judged after you've heard the whole of the evidence. We now do understand that Mr. Harmon puts part of this transcript in relation to evidence not coming from this witness. Mr. Harmon is, to some extent, allowed to choose to use the time that is allotted to him in the way he wants to do that. I would allow Mr. Harmon now to proceed, the matter having been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just make clear what I meant when I said it didn't make sense. I'm not making the point that then in the overall context of the evidence the content of the particular conversation might not make sense fitting in. I'm making the rather more practical point that really, Your Honour, I defy anybody to make much sense of a stream of transcript of an interview where there's absolutely no break between one speaker and another when, necessarily, the same interpreter is speaking and it's simply going onto the transcript as a sort of stream of consciousness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. The Chamber does understand your observation in this respect, that it might not be easy to identify who exactly is speaking at what moment. At the same time, where the -- it becomes clear from this evidence those words, apart from who exactly at any specific moment spoke what word exactly, at least it's a conversation between two gentlemen that have been identified, and the subject, of course, I wouldn't say becomes in every respect clear but at least the subject is known from this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I simply add, we really do express concern, Your Honour, that my client, who is on trial here for genocide and other crimes, that what he says should be more carefully distinguished from what somebody else says. Your Honour's observation that two gentlemen are having a conversation, that really isn't good enough, with respect, to have it absolutely clear and absolutely clear on the transcript. Otherwise we're suggesting it's a waste of time to go through this exercise, if the public transcript does not then make it clear what is said by Mr. Krajisnik who is on trial and what is said by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if not every single word could be allocated to one of the speakers, that doesn't mean that such a conversation between two gentlemen identified would have no evidentiary value at all, Mr. Stewart. If you say that the evidentiary value of a conversation where it's clear what words are exactly spoken by what person, I would easily agree with you that the evidentiary value would be higher, but that doesn't mean that if not every word is clear in the mouth of one of the persons, that the evidentiary value of such a conversation and of a transcript of that conversation is completely lost. Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I'm going to be playing another intercept. This is found at tab 7. This intercept is three minutes and 56 seconds long and it is an intercept from February of 1992. If we could listen to that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo KRAJISNIK: So knackered, you cannot imagine. Radovan KARADZIC: So he's resting or what? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He's not. He's gone down to Reljevo. So down there, people... I'm right, it's a fantastic idea. It's a big territory. They want to establish Rajlovac municipality as it used to be, you know. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's a big territory, so then people want you to sit down with them. I stayed until late last night and I had to go to the Constitutional Commission, so I asked Milos to go. I can't -- but Milos Savic -- Radovan KARADZIC: Ours, Milos Savic, the constitutional one? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Uh-huh. So he went to have a bit of a look, but in any case, we agreed. I thought I'd see what's up with you. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. You see, that's good. We should only -- I should only give you a bit more of advice. I went to see Branko down there last night, but I didn't find him. I found some others, so now he's come to see me. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Which Branko? Radovan KARADZIC: Simic. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Uh-huh. That's what you wanted? No? Radovan KARADZIC: I stayed until late, until 3.00. I actually came at 3.00. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And you didn't meet anyone? Radovan KARADZIC: I did, but not Branko. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Uh-huh. And you didn't find Branko. You didn't -- Radovan KARADZIC: I found some others. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Uh-huh. Radovan KARADZIC: It was very interesting and useful. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Was it? Well, I'm very glad. Radovan KARADZIC: It was even more radical and stuff. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, I'm very glad that it's all right. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: So Branko is not there, is he? Radovan KARADZIC: He's just come to see me. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Ah, well, nice. Radovan KARADZIC: Hmmm. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. It needs to be discussed and agreed on. Radovan KARADZIC: All right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: So what else is new? Radovan KARADZIC: Nothing else. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good. That's the most important thing, isn't it? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes, that's the most important thing. That's what -- today, I think. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Will be much more significant and -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right, I'll see you tomorrow. I just thought I'd call to see what's new. Radovan KARADZIC: All right. What's there tomorrow? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Huh? Radovan KARADZIC: What's there tomorrow? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Nothing. We'll talk a bit tomorrow to see, you know. We have to decide about the Council of Municipalities, so we'll find some sort of a method. But I think that it must if they agree because, you see, I don't know what that Barac, Bakrac, what's his name, Barac doing? Radovan KARADZIC: Yeah. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Did you listen to him? Radovan KARADZIC: From Zenica, right? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. Radovan KARADZIC: Forget about him. He's talking rubbish. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, no. He says they will go, but he says, because the question is changed. Radovan KARADZIC: They, they are changing it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Hmmm? Radovan KARADZIC: They are changing it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah, I'm not clear about that. Radovan KARADZIC: I'll see you, and when I do, we'll have a word. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. Say hi to Branko. Radovan KARADZIC: Okay. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Bye. Radovan KARADZIC: Cheers." "Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Hey, Radovan. Radovan KARADZIC: Eh? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Nikola says that he wilL -- that we should go up there, but there's horrible fog. I think that he's on his way here, but he won't be able to come. Radovan KARADZIC: Come where? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Did he speak to you now? Radovan KARADZIC: He did. I told him to check with you, but I don't know what will -- tonight -- do we have to -- yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There's nothing. I thought he said that he told you that he had to come. Radovan KARADZIC: No, no. I told him to check with you to -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There's no reason. Radovan KARADZIC: I thought I should see what we'll do. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Right. There's no reason, dear God. He asked me something. He said that we should meet. I thought it was an emergency. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: But it looks like it's not. He won't be able to come? There's terrible fog. Radovan KARADZIC: And where would he like to go? To come to my place? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah, yeah. Didn't you agree with him? Radovan KARADZIC: No. I told him to agree with you, if there's a point, to check the concept or something. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, nothing. Radovan KARADZIC: Eh? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: What do we have to do tomorrow, isn't that? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: But there -- that's what I want to tell you, so I thought I couldn't come, because there's horrible fog. Radovan KARADZIC: Did you see the news? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I did. Radovan KARADZIC: Did you see what they --? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I don't know what that is, if we are for independent. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, but they are for changing the question of the three things, three nations, that is, the three entities and so on. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah, yeah, that's good. Radovan KARADZIC: And they are asking for Croatian citizenship. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes, yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's great. Is that the whole? That means all Croats, right? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's great. It will probably ask the Assembly. What will it want? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Well, I think we'll talk. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. There. Radovan KARADZIC: Right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Let me tell you, I'm very sorry if he's left. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: But I don't know. If he comes, it's stupid for us to meet. Something's on his mind, you know. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I thought, by God, I've just spoken to him and he didn't say anything. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He blew it up a bit, but let me tell you, I can't wait to -- this fog, it's horrible. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, I'll tell him now, if he's on his way. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He isn't. I called him at home. Radovan KARADZIC: He hasn't left yet? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He's not there, but he won't be able to come. My aunt paid for the taxi. She says it went? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Eh? Radovan KARADZIC: All right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: In any case, we shouldn't meet. I'll see you tomorrow. Radovan KARADZIC: All right. If he comes, he'll have a cup of coffee and that's it. And I'll see you tomorrow, right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Right."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I proceed with the questions in respect of this intercept, I noticed that the translation of this, I refer to Your Honours to page 60, line 20, has more words in it than the intercept translation that we have tendered. So I will go back to the language assistants and ask them to listen to it once again. I'm referring specifically to the third box from the top on page 1 of the English translation, where it says "he's not -- he's gone down to Reljevo. So down there people... I'm right? is an idea." And if you look at page 60, line 20, you'll see it's slightly different translation with the addition of the word fantastic. So I need to go back and check this translation of this intercept, and if this is incomplete, then I will tender a new document. But I can proceed with my questions on this nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we also observe that it seems to us clearly to be two conversations. There's a break in the middle. Where it says continuation in the middle of the transcript that we've got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you clarify that, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what we're inviting, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, Mr. Cengic. This is an intercept from February, and let me read a portion of this to you and then I'm going to ask you a question. I'm referring to the top of the third box. I will start my reading with Mr. Krajisnik on page 1, part of the way through: "Big territory. They want to establish Rajlovac municipality as it used to be, you know." Karadzic says: "Uh-huh." And Krajisnik says: "That's a big territory, so then people want you to sit down with them. I stayed until late last night and I had to go to the constitutional commission so I asked Milos to go. I can't ... That's Milos Savic." Karadzic: "Ours, the constitutional one?" Krajisnik: "Uh-huh. So he went to have a bit of a look, but in any case, we agreed. I thought I'd see what's up with you." Now, first of all, do you know who Milos Savic is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. In February -- well, let me ask you: By February, had the situation in respect of the new separate commune been resolved?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. If we could turn to the next intercept, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before we continue, may I take it that the continuation issue, the one or two conversations, that you have no immediate clarification but that we'll hear from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When do you expect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As soon as I have. By Wednesday. I will see if I can resolve this very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could play the next intercept, Your Honour. I'm referring to the intercept that is in tab 8 of your binders. And this is a conversation, Your Honours, that is dated February the 22nd, 1992. And one of the speakers is a gentleman by the name of Mr. Karadzic. The other speaker, if I turn to the -- if we can just have a moment. The only voice that was recognised by this witness was Mr. Karadzic's voice. If we could play that intercept, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Ljubo GRKOVIC: For disturbing you. Are we going to print all the flyers or are we going to send some out to the regions? Radovan KARADZIC: And where will they print? Once we agree that the cheapest thing is to print? Ljubo GRKOVIC: All right. I mean, I found everything here and the preparationS are over. We could start printing tonight and have everything ready tomorrow. Radovan KARADZIC: We need to check. We need to check once again how much it costs. Going out there means helping -- Ljubo GRKOVIC: Them? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, helping them to create a sovereign independent Bosnia and Herzegovina in which we would be slaves. The Serbs won't participate, won't vote. The flyer seems good to me, but I can't remember --? Ljubo GRKOVIC: Yes, yes, some correction may be necessary. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Ljubo GRKOVIC: When I bring them, will you have a look at them? One copy has already been made. Radovan KARADZIC: Printed, right? Ljubo GRKOVIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Please bring a copy. Ljubo GRKOVIC: I'll do that later. I've just arrived from Reljevo. We established a municipality down there, do you know that? Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Ljubo GRKOVIC: In Rajlovac. I was there and Joja. It was nice. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Ljubo GRKOVIC: So in an hour or two I might ... Radovan KARADZIC: How many inhabitants will it have? That'll be in Rajlovac, right? Ljubo GRKOVIC: It will be called Rajlovac Serb municipality and it includes Reljevo and everything up till Vogosca and Ilijas, and over here up to Osijek and the television. Radovan KARADZIC: Does it include Vogosca Serb municipality or not? Ljubo GRKOVIC: No, Vogosca will be different. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Ljubo GRKOVIC: Vogosca will be a second unit. This goes up to Vogosca, right down to Joja's house. Radovan KARADZIC: And then all the way to Ilijas, right? Ljubo GRKOVIC: This way it includes Gras, around the television, but it doesn't include the television. Then it goes down towards Odzakovici and so. Radovan KARADZIC: And these are all Serb areas, right? Ljubo GRKOVIC: Yes, a large area. Not densely populated, but a large area. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Good. Ljubo GRKOVIC: You'll be at home, right? Radovan KARADZIC: I will, I will. Ljubo GRKOVIC: Okay, I'll drop by in an hour or two. Radovan KARADZIC: Okay, I may be sleeping then. It would be better if saw each other around six. Ljubo GRKOVIC: I can, I can fax it to you so you can look at it. Radovan KARADZIC: All right, all right. Ljubo GRKOVIC: Is that, is that 32? Radovan KARADZIC: It is. Ljubo GRKOVIC: 029. Radovan KARADZIC: I'll see you. Cheers. Ljubo GRKOVIC: All the best, Doctor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I take it that you make a similar comment on the completeness of the transcript in the third box. No, I think in the second box there's something about costs which doesn't appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll check that as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Possible, of course, a possible explanation might be that our interpreters do even hear better than those who made the transcript of this intercept. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, this is a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Ljubo Grkovic. Do you know who Mr. Grkovic is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this particular intercept, this conversation was intercepted on February 22nd, 1992. On the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992, there was a referendum in which the citizens of Bosnia were asked if they were in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So according to this conversation, the municipality, the Serb municipality of Rajlovac, was established at least in principle by February 22nd. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: No, I was not. But if I may, I should like to comment a portion of this conversation where it is indicated that the area is not densely populated, that there are not many inhabitants living there. Now, I have heard this conversation for the first time these days, but now I am able to understand it better. The fact that they counted the population, although that number was not precise, in light of that, I can claim that there is over 20.000 inhabitants living in the area. And more than 70 per cent of them are Bosniak. The area described here includes several local communes, Reljevo, Rajlovac, and also a number of other local communes that are not specifically mentioned but are included in the area, such as Brijesce, Boljakov Potok, Buca Potok, Dolac. So if one should take into account all of this information, we can conclude that there is a large number of people living there, the majority of whom were Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, let me turn my attention to a different subject, and that is this: Are you aware of Mr. Krajisnik coming to the municipality of Novi Grad; and if so, under what circumstances are you aware?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: The offices of all parties represented in the parliament, those who had their representatives in the Municipal Assembly, were located in the town hall, and the municipal building. I was from time to time informed of those meetings, and it is my impression that Mr. Krajisnik was very often the guest of the SDS offices in the town hall, that he often went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was it reported to you that he appeared at the town hall by others?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: It is customary for the employees of the town hall, when they finish their work for the day, for a record to be taken of the people entering and leaving the building. Those who are not employees of the town hall. And such information should have been kept by the janitor. But it was also from time to time that the SDA people informed me of that fact, because they had an office in the immediate vicinity to their office. I didn't ascribe much importance to these visits at the time, but I took note of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And let me put these visits in context, because my question was a little imprecise. When I asked you if he had come to the municipality frequently, I'm talking about the period before the commencement of the war. Do you understand that, and would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, of course. Before the war. No. Before the war began, he never -- he no longer came. But up to the commencement of the war. Because after the war, that was controlled by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to another intercept, Mr. Cengic. This is found at tab 3. This is an intercept from the date of 8 November, 1991. This intercept is 5 minutes and 9 seconds long.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Radovan KARADZIC: Okay. What are you doing? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, to tell you the truth, a little bit of everything and so forth. Radovan KARADZIC: I barely got up this morning, could hardly get up. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, one gets tired. Last night my legs hurt. Fuck it. I could only lean my legs against the wall. Radovan KARADZIC: Me too, but it's from the tension. I felt slightly responsible; not slightly but a lot, you know. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I can tell you that yesterday you were not in form. I saw that earlier. You had some -- you know, you were -- you were tense. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes, you're right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Because I was considerably concerned as to whether it would succeed. I was considerably worried. I cannot rely on Jovo entirely. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I know, you can't rely on anyone. Radovan KARADZIC: You can't rely on anyone and then you know. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I can tell you, you were not in form. Radovan KARADZIC: I wasn't. That wasn't how I really speak; I speak better. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: But I think it's important that it didn't fall beyond certain standards. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. I hope that it wasn't bad. Only Yutel, fuck them, they took out all those inserts, you know. Radovan KARADZIC: That's right, that's right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And so it goes. Radovan KARADZIC: That's right. But they're basically not bad, I can tell you. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Is that right? Radovan KARADZIC: I watched Yutel. It basically isn't bad. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. Radovan KARADZIC: I don't know how it was presented on the third programme. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I didn't watch. Radovan KARADZIC: On the third programme, news programme. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I didn't watch anything, so I have no idea. Radovan KARADZIC: Ljilja says it was short, there was no -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, yes. First they cut 20 minutes and then 15. You know that shortens it. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Now, look here, tonight there will be something on the news. We have a time slot. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: We have 5 minutes. Ekmecic isn't there. Do you want to appear, to explain it? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, I can do it. It's not a problem. Radovan KARADZIC: And Aco is going somewhere else. I don't know where he's going. Aco is going to Yutel. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: What I wanted to do is, I wanted to be completely angry at them. Radovan KARADZIC: At whom? The television? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: The television? Radovan KARADZIC: All right, but don't. Your cheerfulness should come to the fore, because of our people, you know. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right, I will if you think so, but I thought that I would remain until the end. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, but we'll take advantage of things, you know. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: We must take advantage of it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who is the editor? Radovan KARADZIC: Of this evening's news? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: I have no idea. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right, I will -- Radovan KARADZIC: You know what would be very important, for you to make an appearance and Aco will go to Yutel. Aco, has he been in touch with you? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He hasn't. He'll probably call me. Radovan KARADZIC: You know what? We anticipate that our people are thinking about now, it would be necessary to influence their opinion. So don't say anywhere that you are afraid. On the contrary. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, no it's out of the question. What Biljana said was not all right. That is... Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I didn't agree with that at all. Radovan KARADZIC: On the contrary; that is a democratic way of voicing our opinion. This is the only way to preserve peace, so everyone can say what they are in favour of. You're intelligent. You will do it. Just stay cheerful and triumphant. Do you understand? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Of course, certainly. I saw how much that means to people. People don't like it when you tell them that their state is happy. They'd rather die than... Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Just be cheerful and triumphant. There's no other way. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's right. Radovan KARADZIC: And... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right, I will. But where is Ekmecic? He is gone. Radovan KARADZIC: I think he's gone. But you, I think it would be a good thing if you were to... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will. There's no problem. Radovan KARADZIC: I'll call you, but let him call them, and then you need to say don't. You know what else: Citizens do not need to think at all about polling stations. Let them vote wherever they are. Let them vote wherever they are with just a personal identity card. It can be done in a local commune, it can be done in a village if someone is away for the weekend. Everything acceptable, only just let them vote. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I'll see now with that fellow that there is a bit more -- that simply, now I'll call that fellow, only I don't know who the editor is. Can Ljubo check it out and let me know? Radovan KARADZIC: He can. I think so. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Let him see who he is, who it is. You know, I wouldn't want to do this intentionally. Let them inform them that I'll come and then I'll get in touch with them. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Maybe you will get a bit more space to explain what the goals are and that the Muslims and Croats should come out and that it's not -- no one's going anywhere. They say like you're going in Bosnia. No one's going anywhere. It's only a question of how we will arrange things so we can live with each other, live next to each other, and how we will manage our affairs. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, certainly I will. There's no problem. I think I will take it and go. Only tell me: What was your impression last night? Radovan KARADZIC: I think that it was all right. Essentially, it was all right. I mean, I can be dissatisfied with my form, but everything else was excellent. Right, right basically, essentially it was excellent. I can tell you because you saw how the public reacts, you know. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, yes, that's the main thing. I hope that is all right. Radovan KARADZIC: Right, right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We must get ready tomorrow and organise everything well so that everything turns out all right. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. The press centre down there and up there and the polling-stations and so forth. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Will there be a press centre? Radovan KARADZIC: The press centre is in the Holiday Inn. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You will vote tomorrow at 11.00, right? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I said I would go over to Zabrdje to see what was going on. What is it, a journalist? Is that right? Radovan KARADZIC: You'll vote in Zabrdje, right? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I'm supposed to do it in Zabrdje. Radovan KARADZIC: All right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will organise things for my people so that it turns out the right way. Radovan KARADZIC: All right. That's okay. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You're at home? Radovan KARADZIC: No, I'm not. I'm at the clinic. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. We'll be in touch. Radovan KARADZIC: Okay. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I'll go over there. Radovan KARADZIC: All right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Goodbye. Radovan KARADZIC: Bye."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I tried to follow the French translation. I think we have to pay specific attention to the French translation. It goes so quick that I got the impression, but of course I can't check it on paper because I have no French transcript, that sometimes not every single line could be translated in due time. So we have to find a solution for that so that we have a complete French transcript. May I ask the French interpreters whether my impression is true. Yes. It is confirmed to me by the French interpreters that my impression was right. So we have to pay specific attention to that. But that's not a reason at this moment not to continue. But I just wanted to have that on the record. Mr. Harmon, perhaps you first put questions in relation to this transcript to the witness and then stop for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Two questions, Mr. Cengic. You recognise -- do you recognise -- did you -- you have already recognised the voices of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik in this intercept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This intercept is dated on the 8th of November, 1991. It is correct, is it not, Mr. Cengic, that on the 9th and the 10th of November, 1991, there was a Bosnian Serb plebiscite in which question was asked whether the voters wished to stay in the joint state of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the plebiscite in question, or rather, the conversation concerns the plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions about this particular intercept, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until 5 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please escort the witness into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I can explain to the parties that we start a bit late because the translation issue was of some concern, because it now turned out that not only the French interpreters could not follow the speed of the English text, which they have in writing in front of them, but even that the English interpreters were not always able to pronounce all the words that they hear in B/C/S version. So, therefore, some of the text is missing. And we have to find a solution for that, Mr. Harmon, but you might be approached for that problem one of these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I already have, Your Honour, and I'm going to meet tomorrow morning with people from the language service section to try to find a solution that would be satisfactory to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please be aware that I gave a call to Mr. Pimentel, who is finally responsible for transcripts, I think, and I also discussed the matter with at least some of the translators involved today. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, let me ask you: Based on your contacts with Mr. Krajisnik before the war, your contact with Serbs in the community both before and during the war, and your knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik in the other communities, Bosniak and Croat communities, where would you rank Mr. Krajisnik in the hierarchy of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: In my opinion and the opinion of my friends, Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic are at the same level within this hierarchy, whereas all the others are far away from them in the line, far down the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And where -- at what level are they in that hierarchy, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: They are the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn my attention to another time period, and that is the time period after the Dayton Peace Accords. Following the signing of the Dayton peace agreements, Mr. Cengic, did you have an opportunity to go to the Rajlovac municipality and did you meet with Serbs from that community?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: The German department of the UNPROFOR made it possible for me, as president of the Novi Grad municipality, to visit the then-Serb municipality of Novi Grad and meet the citizens. Actually, I made a mistake. It was the municipality of Rajlovac that I was referring to. So I was to meet the inhabitants of the Rajlovac municipality in a building that housed the distribution centre before the war. That's where at that time the Rajlovac municipality structures were situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date when you had that meeting with the Serbs from the Serb community of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: It was some two to three days before the actual integration was to take place. I think it was the 26th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do you remember with whom you met, by name, the individuals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if we are that far away, I'd rather have a year. 26th of February of 1990 --?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. Oh, rather, 1996, after the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: February, immediately after the Dayton Agreement. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, do you remember the names of the people with whom you met, or some of the names of the people with whom you met?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the names, because the meeting was a brief one. We did introduce ourselves, but I cannot recall the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the purpose of having this meeting, Mr. Cengic, and on whose initiative was the meeting established?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, at the initiative of a group of Serbs who wanted to remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: I myself, the chief of police, and UNPROFOR representatives arrived there and were met by the representatives of the Serbs. We sat at a table and discussed the future. And on that occasion, I promised that I would do my best for those citizens of the Rajlovac municipality who remained there to have their security ensured. And as for the general logistics, support, support in general, that we would share the same destiny, because the situation was very difficult in terms of food supplies and the rest. It was the end of the war, and we hardly had anything left. And I said that what we do or do not have, we are going to share it all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did the representatives of the Serb community explain to you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: They said that they were willing to stay there but that, however, they had Mr. Krajisnik's order that all of them had to move out, that they had to take all of their belongings with them that they could take, so that people went as far as taking windows and doors off their houses together with them, and whatever could be taken from the factories was actually taken at that point and whatever could not be taken was set on fire. And here I'm referring to those Serbs who were leaving. Some of the Serbs remained, and subsequently, they found themselves in a more favourable position compared to the Serbs who had left and then returned, because their houses were intact, whereas the Serbs who were leaving destroyed their own houses themselves by dismantling doors and windows and the rest. This way, very expensive equipment was taken from this area that used to be very rich, from the aeroplane engines factory, Orao, whatever could be taken from the distribution centre, from the bakery, the local bakery, and other important plants, like, for instance, the Rajlovac depot, was taken. And I emphasise that whatever could not be taken was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, did you have an opportunity personally to hear Mr. Krajisnik express views as to multi-ethnic life in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, or rather, those of us in Sarajevo who were lucky enough to have the electricity, we listened to the radio, and I myself had personally on several occasions heard Karadzic express anger at the fact that the agreement had been signed. And every time he did speak, it was obvious that he recommended and even in a way threatened the Serbian people that they had to leave the areas and even take the dead who were buried there with them from these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cengic, the question that I asked you was: Did you have an opportunity personally to hear Mr. Krajisnik express views as to multi-ethnic life in Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: On the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And -- Mr. Cengic, let me repeat what I said. My question to you was: Did you have an opportunity personally to hear Mr. Krajisnik express views as to multi-ethnic life in Bosnia. Your answer was: On several occasions, or rather, those of us in Sarajevo who were lucky enough to have electricity, we listened to the radio, and I myself had personally on several occasions heard Karadzic express anger at the fact that the agreement had been signed."

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Krajisnik. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So what reads presently in your answer "Mr. Karadzic" should read "Mr. Krajisnik"; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course, Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate dates when you heard these comments by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: This was mostly after the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords and it was on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember -- was this -- these comments that you heard, that you attribute to Mr. Krajisnik, did you hear those on the radio, on the television? What was the media source for those sorts of comments that you recall?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC
utterances.text: It was SRNA, the Serbian information agency. And mostly on television and sometimes on the radio as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I've concluded my examination. Thank you very much, Your Honour s. I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Stewart, do I understand that you have agreed more or less that you would start cross-examination tomorrow or would you rather start now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands, but yes, that's what we did discuss earlier, and we came to the conclusion that shouldn't present any real difficulties as far as the overall timetable is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you couldn't start, the Chamber would accept that at this moment. On the other hand, in order to avoid whatever risk, and it might be anything like the air-conditioning not functioning tomorrow or whatever happens, the Chamber would really like to avoid, to the extent possible, that we would not finish with the witnesses this week. So the Chamber would prefer, and I say it in this way, that you'd start your cross-examination now. But at the same time, sometimes one can feel the difference in weight on invitations. I leave it up to you whether you'd start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I didn't wish to disguise the fact that I hadn't expected and am not ready to begin cross-examination efficiently today. The estimate was four and a half hours in chief here. So, Your Honour, I don't wish to be -- I don't wish to disguise that in making that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you not only have a preference to start tomorrow but a very strong preference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour could put it exactly that way and I wouldn't disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other hand, you may have noticed that, and Mr. Harmon as well, that if tomorrow or the day after tomorrow the air-conditioning would not function, this Chamber will certainly try a solution to nevertheless finish with the witnesses of this week, whether we have to find another courtroom or -- so we'll be stronger than usual in finding solutions if your confidence would turn out to be not realistic. I include all circumstances of life, not only that you are performing under what we could expect, but whatever circumstance there will be there, the Chamber will try to finish the three witnesses and at the same time now follows your wish and allow you to start cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I observe this, Your Honour, that generally speaking cross-examinations that start first thing at the beginning of a day finish at around the same time as cross-examinations that start half an hour before the close of a day. That's just a fact of life. They do tend to finish at the same time anyway. So the time doesn't really get lost normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This observation is something the parties should think over what the consequences are of this fact of life, because it means that sometimes you can do an examination of a witness a bit quicker if you have less time. Mr. Cengic, we'll finish for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom again. You'll then be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence. I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and you're still about to give tomorrow. We adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00.
